title: AF-6-part-2
description: Airframe exam covering aircraft pressurization and oxygen systems: outflow/relief/dump valves, pressurization control modes, cabin altitude and differential pressure, oxygen storage and regulator types, and related safety and maintenance considerations, drawn from the AF-6 pressurization/oxygen systems question/answer bank.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of using turbocharger/supercharger-based cabin pressurization (rather than clean bleed air)?
options: B. Risk of contamination (exhaust gases or oil) entering the cabin air supply
C. Inability to pressurize at all
questions.explanation: Turbocharger/supercharger-sourced air can carry contaminants such as oil fumes or exhaust gases, posing a cabin air quality and safety risk compared with dedicated clean bleed air.

questions.question: How many fail-safe provisions/systems are typically designed into an aircraft pressurization system?
questions.explanation: Pressurization systems are commonly designed with multiple (often three) layers of fail-safe protection, such as automatic, standby, and manual/relief valve backups.

questions.question: What provides automatic control of pressurization using an alternate input source when the primary system fails?
questions.explanation: The standby mode automatically takes over pressurization control, using backup sensors/logic, if the primary automatic controller fails.

questions.question: What instrument indicates the rate of cabin pressure change?
options: A. The cabin vertical speed indicator
questions.explanation: A cabin vertical speed (rate of climb/descent) indicator shows how quickly the cabin's equivalent altitude is changing, in feet per minute.

questions.question: What does the dump valve do during descent or after landing?
options: A. It opens and releases cabin pressure to the atmosphere
B. It closes to seal the cabin completely
questions.explanation: The dump valve, when activated, fully opens to quickly vent remaining cabin pressure to ambient, typically used during descent/landing or emergencies.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the aircraft cabin pressurizing system?
options: B. To make the cabin environment comfortable and safe for occupants at altitude
questions.explanation: Cabin pressurization maintains a physiologically comfortable and safe cabin altitude, allowing passengers and crew to function normally despite high cruise altitudes.

questions.question: Below what altitude is additional (supplemental) oxygen generally not required for occupants?
options: B. 15,000 ft (varies by specific regulation, but commonly referenced threshold)
questions.explanation: Regulatory thresholds specify altitudes above which supplemental oxygen becomes mandatory; below the specified altitude (commonly cited around this range), it is typically not required.

questions.question: What prevents cabin altitude from becoming higher (cabin pressure lower) than the aircraft's actual altitude?
options: A. The negative pressure relief valve
B. The positive pressure relief valve
questions.explanation: A negative relief valve opens if outside pressure exceeds cabin pressure (e.g., during rapid descent), preventing the cabin from being at a lower pressure than ambient, which could otherwise damage the structure inward.

questions.question: Which component prevents overpressurization of the oxygen system after the oxygen has been regulated?
questions.explanation: A safety relief valve downstream of the pressure reducer protects the lower-pressure portion of the oxygen system from overpressure if the reducer fails.

questions.question: During which phase of flight is the negative pressure relief valve primarily relied upon?
questions.explanation: Rapid descent can cause outside pressure to rise faster than cabin pressure can equalize, making the negative relief valve important during this phase to prevent reverse pressure differential damage.

questions.question: Which component is used to cool pressurized (bleed) air before it enters the cabin?
questions.explanation: A heat exchanger removes heat from hot bleed air using ram air cooling, preparing the air for cabin distribution at an appropriate temperature.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of a typical isobaric (constant-altitude) pressurization control system?
questions.explanation: An eccentric cam valve is not a standard isobaric pressurization system component; the system is built around the outflow valve and pressure controller instead.

questions.question: During what phase of flight is the outflow valve normally closed?
questions.explanation: During the takeoff roll, the outflow valve is commanded closed in preparation for pressurization to begin as the aircraft lifts off and climbs.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT used to equalize cabin pressure to ambient pressure during landing?
options: B. Takeoff mode (a different operating mode, not used for landing equalization)
C. The outflow valve opening fully
questions.explanation: Takeoff mode configures the system for departure, not for equalizing pressure during landing; a separate landing/ground logic handles that function.

questions.question: Which oxygen storage method contains the largest amount of oxygen per equal unit (volume/weight)?
questions.explanation: Liquid oxygen is far more energy-dense (more oxygen molecules per unit volume/weight) than compressed gaseous oxygen, though it requires cryogenic storage.

questions.question: Which of the following requires human intervention to operate?
options: A. The outflow valve (in automatic mode)
questions.explanation: Unlike automatically operating valves, a dump valve is typically manually activated by the crew when rapid depressurization is desired.

questions.question: In turbine-engine aircraft, where does the pressurization air come from?
options: A. A dedicated electric air compressor only
questions.explanation: Turbine engines readily supply high-pressure, high-temperature bleed air from the compressor section, which is tapped and conditioned for cabin pressurization.

questions.question: At approximately what cabin altitude does the cabin altitude warning (red) light typically extinguish once pressure is restored?
questions.explanation: As cabin altitude descends back below the warning threshold (commonly around 8,500-10,000 ft depending on aircraft type), the cabin altitude warning light extinguishes.

questions.question: In all-pneumatic cabin pressure regulator and outflow valve systems, which line serves as a pressure sensing/reference connection related to venting?
questions.explanation: The dump valve's associated sensing connection feeds pressure reference information used by the pneumatic regulator logic in older all-pneumatic systems.

questions.question: Cabin pressure expressed in real time is most directly represented by what measurement?
options: B. Barometric (absolute) pressure within the cabin
questions.explanation: Cabin pressure is fundamentally a barometric pressure measurement, which is then converted into the more intuitive cabin altitude readout for crew display.

questions.question: What is the main difference between pressure demand and diluter demand oxygen systems?
options: A. A diluter demand system delivers oxygen at higher pressure
B. A pressure demand system can deliver oxygen at higher pressure than a diluter demand system
C. There is no functional difference
questions.explanation: Pressure demand regulators can supply oxygen under positive pressure (useful at very high altitudes), unlike diluter demand regulators, which mix oxygen with cabin air at closer to ambient pressure.

questions.question: What color is the overpressure discharge (blowout) disk typically marked or made from?
questions.explanation: A green plastic/colored discharge indicator disk is commonly used so maintenance personnel can easily see if an oxygen system has discharged due to overpressure.

questions.question: At high altitude, how does fuel consumption typically compare with lower altitude flight, for the same aircraft/power setting?
options: C. Less (more fuel-efficient at altitude, generally)
questions.explanation: Aircraft generally achieve better fuel efficiency at higher cruise altitudes due to reduced air density and drag, within their designed flight envelope.

questions.question: How is ground pressurization and leakage of the fuselage typically checked?
options: A. With a static (ground) pressure test
B. By flying a test flight only
questions.explanation: A static pressure test conducted on the ground pressurizes the fuselage to check for leaks and verify seal integrity, without needing an actual flight.

questions.question: What drives the compressor in a turbine-engine-based pressurization system (such as a bootstrap air cycle system)?
options: A. A separate electric motor only
B. The landing gear wheel rotation
C. Engine bleed air driving a turbine, which in turn drives the compressor
questions.explanation: In a bootstrap air cycle system, hot engine bleed air expands through a turbine, and that turbine's rotation mechanically drives an attached compressor.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of a jet pump (ejector) based air system on an aircraft?
options: A. It cannot move air at all
B. It requires no bleed air
C. Its relatively low efficiency in managing environmental volume/pressure compared with other methods
questions.explanation: Jet pump (venturi-based ejector) systems, while simple, are relatively inefficient at managing larger air volumes/pressures compared with dedicated compressors or valves.

questions.question: Which pressure-controlling valve/component is used to make a smooth transition from unpressurized to pressurized cabin operation during takeoff?
options: B. The throttle position switch (sensing takeoff power application)
questions.explanation: A throttle position switch senses when takeoff power is applied, triggering the pressurization system to begin its smooth transition into pressurized operation.

questions.question: Which air system utilizes the Venturi effect?
questions.explanation: A jet pump/flow multiplier uses the Venturi effect, where a high-velocity jet of air entrains and multiplies the flow of additional air drawn alongside it.

questions.question: If the oxygen reducer (pressure-reducing) valve fails, what maintains safe downstream pressure?
questions.explanation: A relief valve downstream of the reducer provides backup protection, venting excess pressure if the reducer valve fails and allows pressure to rise too high.

questions.question: Which type of oxygen system is least complicated and requires the least maintenance?
questions.explanation: Chemical oxygen generators have no moving parts, pressure vessels, or plumbing to maintain, making them simple, low-maintenance (though single-use) oxygen sources.

questions.question: What device reduces oxygen pressure from a high storage pressure down to a lower usable pressure?
questions.explanation: The reducer valve steps down the high pressure of stored oxygen (in the cylinder) to a safer, lower working pressure for distribution to the system.

questions.question: An oxygen cylinder is generally considered empty/needing service when its pressure drops to approximately what value?
options: C. 0 psi exactly, with no margin
questions.explanation: A residual minimum pressure, such as around 50 psi, is typically used as the threshold indicating the cylinder needs recharging, even though it isn't literally at zero.

questions.question: What indicates the pressure remaining in a portable oxygen cylinder?
options: A. A pressure gauge mounted on the portable cylinder
questions.explanation: A portable oxygen cylinder includes its own integral pressure gauge, allowing a direct check of remaining oxygen pressure/quantity.

questions.question: Which component, controlled by the landing gear squat switch, is commanded to open when the aircraft is on the ground?
questions.explanation: The squat switch signals ground status, commanding the dump valve open to ensure the cabin is unpressurized/depressurized while on the ground.

questions.question: How is the serviceability of an oxygen cylinder's pressure system typically verified during a leak/burst test?
options: A. By testing (submerging/checking) with water to observe for bubbles or verify integrity
questions.explanation: A water bath/immersion test can be used to check for leaks (bubbles) or to conduct hydrostatic testing to verify the cylinder's structural serviceability.

questions.question: Which component removes (releases) all positive cabin pressure, such as for ground maintenance or emergency use?
options: B. The outflow valve alone in normal mode
questions.explanation: Activating the dump valve releases all remaining positive cabin pressure quickly, bringing the cabin to ambient pressure.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the outflow valve?
options: A. To supply bleed air into the cabin
B. To maintain the desired cabin pressure by controlling how much air exits the cabin
C. To cool the cabin air
questions.explanation: The outflow valve modulates the rate at which pressurized air is allowed to escape the cabin overboard, thereby controlling and maintaining the desired cabin pressure.

questions.question: Which cockpit indicators are typically part of the cabin pressurization display?
options: A. Engine RPM, EGT, and oil pressure
B. Airspeed, heading, and altitude only
C. Cabin altitude, cabin rate of climb, and differential pressure
questions.explanation: Standard pressurization instrumentation displays cabin altitude, the rate of cabin altitude change, and the pressure differential between cabin and ambient.

questions.question: How is pressurization control fundamentally achieved?
options: A. By controlling engine RPM directly
B. By controlling the amount of air going out of the airplane (via the outflow valve)
C. By controlling landing gear position
questions.explanation: Because bleed air continuously enters the cabin, pressurization is managed by metering how much air is allowed to exit through the outflow valve.

questions.question: Where is the BITE (Built-In Test Equipment) function for pressurization typically accessed?
options: A. On the landing gear control panel
B. On the cabin pressure controller
questions.explanation: The cabin pressure controller incorporates its own BITE test function, allowing technicians to run diagnostic checks directly from that unit.

questions.question: What does it mean when "ALTN" (alternate) is displayed/indicated on the pressurization system?
options: A. That the normal (primary) mode is faulty and the system has switched to alternate/standby control
B. That the aircraft is above its maximum altitude
C. That the oxygen system has discharged
questions.explanation: An ALTN indication shows that the primary automatic pressurization controller has a fault, and the system has transferred control to its backup/alternate controller.

questions.question: Which type of oxygen system does not shut off (stop producing oxygen) before it is fully expended?
options: C. The solid chemical oxygen generator
questions.explanation: Once activated, a chemical oxygen generator undergoes a continuous exothermic reaction producing oxygen until the chemical core is fully consumed; it cannot be shut off early.

questions.question: What does the discharge indicator disk on an oxygen bottle (cylinder) reveal?
options: A. That the cylinder is fully charged
B. That the cylinder needs painting
C. That overpressure relief has occurred (the disk has ruptured)
questions.explanation: A ruptured (discharged) green disk visually indicates the cylinder's thermal/overpressure relief device has activated, releasing pressure due to an overpressure condition.

questions.question: What primary control does setting the cabin pressure (selecting a target cabin altitude) affect?
questions.explanation: Selecting a target cabin pressure/altitude directly commands the outflow valve's modulation to achieve and hold that pressure.

questions.question: Pressure measured along a scale that has zero value at a complete vacuum is called what?
questions.explanation: Absolute pressure references true zero (a perfect vacuum), unlike gauge pressure, which references ambient atmospheric pressure as its zero point.

questions.question: What is the typical high storage pressure range for gaseous (compressed) aviation oxygen cylinders?
questions.explanation: Gaseous oxygen storage cylinders for aviation use are commonly charged to a high pressure range around 1,800 to 2,000 psi.

questions.question: What are the typical operating modes of a cabin pressurization controller?
options: A. Unpressurized, isobaric, and differential (constant differential) modes
B. Takeoff, cruise, and landing only
C. Auto, manual, and emergency only
questions.explanation: A pressurization controller typically cycles through unpressurized (ground), isobaric (constant cabin altitude), and differential (constant differential pressure) modes as the flight progresses.

questions.question: During ground operation, how is the cabin pressurization system kept depressurized (open)?
options: B. By a manual pilot switch only, with no automatic logic
C. By a fuel quantity sensor
questions.explanation: A landing gear (weight-on-wheels) operated switch signals ground status, which the pressurization system uses to keep the outflow/dump valve open while on the ground.

questions.question: Continuous flow oxygen delivery is most commonly used for what purpose?
options: C. Portable walk-around bottles for crew
questions.explanation: Continuous flow regulators are simpler and adequate for passengers' intermittent, shorter-duration use, making them the common choice for passenger oxygen masks.

questions.question: Which oxygen storage type is NOT well suited for typical commercial airline use?
questions.explanation: Liquid oxygen requires cryogenic handling and specialized ground support infrastructure, making it less practical for routine commercial airline operations compared with gaseous or chemical systems.

questions.question: What happens to the outflow valve and dump (blow) switch when the aircraft is on the ground after landing?
options: A. They open to allow remaining cabin pressure to vent out to ambient
B. They close to seal the cabin
C. They have no function on the ground
questions.explanation: On the ground, the outflow valve and dump switch function together to open fully, releasing any remaining cabin pressure to equalize with outside ambient pressure.

questions.question: During which flight phase is the cabin altitude typically lower than the airport field altitude?
options: A. The takeoff roll (cabin already slightly pressurized/sealed ahead of climb)
questions.explanation: As the pressurization system begins sealing the cabin in preparation for climb during the takeoff roll, the cabin can briefly register an altitude slightly lower than the actual field elevation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of sealant and grommets used in fuselage construction?
options: A. To reduce aircraft weight significantly
C. To make the aircraft structure airtight
questions.explanation: Sealant and grommets close gaps around fasteners, wiring pass-throughs, and joints, helping maintain the airtight integrity needed for cabin pressurization.

questions.question: How is pressurization typically managed on modern aircraft?
options: A. Only manually, with no automatic function
B. Fully automatically, with manual backup available
C. Only by ground crew before each flight
questions.explanation: Modern pressurization systems operate fully automatically during normal flight, computing and adjusting outflow valve position continuously, with manual control as a backup.

questions.question: What term describes the rate at which cabin altitude changes?
options: B. Cabin rate of change (cabin climb/descent rate)
questions.explanation: Cabin rate of change describes how quickly the cabin's equivalent altitude is rising or falling, analogous to the aircraft's own vertical speed.

questions.question: What does a rate of climb/descent (vertical speed) indicator show?
options: A. Vertical speed in feet per minute
questions.explanation: A vertical speed indicator displays the rate of altitude change, expressed in feet per minute, whether for the aircraft itself or, separately, for cabin altitude.

questions.question: Which of the following is FALSE regarding cabin rate of climb?
options: A. That cabin pressure increases as cabin rate of climb occurs (actually, cabin pressure decreases as cabin altitude climbs)
B. That cabin rate of climb is measured in feet per minute
C. That excessive cabin rate of climb can cause passenger discomfort
questions.explanation: As cabin altitude climbs (a positive cabin rate of climb), cabin pressure actually decreases, not increases, making this statement false.

questions.question: Which pressurization mode allows the crew to control the outflow valve directly?
questions.explanation: In manual mode, the crew directly commands outflow valve position using a cockpit control, bypassing the automatic controller logic.

questions.question: What does it mean if cabin differential pressure is not maintained within limits?
options: A. The differential pressure relief valve has opened, releasing excess pressure
B. The aircraft has exceeded maximum speed
C. The landing gear has failed to retract
questions.explanation: If differential pressure exceeds its safe limit, the differential pressure relief valve opens automatically to vent excess pressure and protect the structure.

questions.question: What pressure range does the oxygen pressure-reducing valve typically reduce storage pressure down to?
questions.explanation: The reducer valve steps high-pressure storage oxygen (around 1,800-2,000 psi) down to a lower working pressure, commonly in the range of about 60-80 psi, for system distribution.

questions.question: During what pressurization mode is cabin pressure maintained at a constant (specific) cabin altitude even as flight altitude changes (within a range)?
questions.explanation: Isobaric mode holds the cabin at a fixed selected altitude (constant pressure) as the aircraft climbs or descends through a range of altitudes, until differential limits are reached.

questions.question: What happens when a specific cabin altitude is selected on the cabin altitude selector?
options: A. It controls isobaric (constant cabin altitude) operation at that selected value
B. It immediately opens the dump valve
C. It shuts down the pressurization system
questions.explanation: Selecting a cabin altitude sets the target value the system will hold constant during isobaric mode operation as the aircraft changes actual altitude.

questions.question: Is it true that the rate of cabin climb controls the rate of cabin pressure change?
options: A. False; they are entirely unrelated
B. False; cabin rate of climb only matters on the ground
questions.explanation: Cabin rate of climb and cabin pressure change rate are directly related; as commanded cabin climb rate increases, cabin pressure falls proportionally faster.

questions.question: What is the purpose of barometric correction in the pressurization system?
options: A. To correct engine fuel flow for altitude
B. To correct the landing field altitude setting for the actual barometric pressure condition at the destination
C. To correct the outflow valve's manufacturing tolerance
questions.explanation: Barometric correction adjusts the system's landing altitude reference to account for actual local barometric pressure at the destination airport, ensuring accurate cabin pressure scheduling for landing.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an input to the cabin pressure regulator/controller?
options: A. Aircraft altitude (the regulator primarily uses cabin pressure/altitude and landing field data, not raw aircraft altitude as a direct control input)
questions.explanation: The pressure controller's core logic is based on cabin pressure/altitude feedback and landing field elevation setting, rather than directly using the aircraft's own altitude as a primary control input.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding continuous flow oxygen systems?
options: A. It is used exclusively for flight crew
B. It delivers oxygen only on demand (inhale-triggered)
C. It is used in the passenger oxygen system
questions.explanation: Continuous flow oxygen delivery, simpler and less precise than demand systems, is the standard choice for passenger oxygen masks in an emergency.

questions.question: Why is an oxygen system installed on a pressurized aircraft, even though the cabin is normally pressurized?
options: B. As a precaution and for first-aid purposes, in case of a pressurization failure or decompression
C. To cool the cabin air
questions.explanation: Oxygen systems provide essential backup protection in case the pressurization system fails or a rapid decompression occurs, as well as for medical/first-aid use.

questions.question: Which of the following is a continuous-supply type of oxygen source?
options: B. The solid chemical generator type
questions.explanation: A chemical oxygen generator, once activated, provides a continuous (non-demand) flow of oxygen until its chemical reaction is complete.

questions.question: What term expresses cabin pressure in terms of the equivalent altitude above sea level the pressure corresponds to?
questions.explanation: Cabin altitude converts the actual cabin air pressure into the equivalent standard atmosphere altitude that would produce that same pressure, giving an intuitive reference.

questions.question: What is the ratio (or difference) between inside and outside air pressures called?
questions.explanation: Differential pressure specifically refers to the difference between cabin (inside) pressure and ambient (outside) pressure, a key parameter in pressurization design and limits.

questions.question: In a diluter-demand oxygen regulator, when does the demand valve operate (admit oxygen)?
options: B. When the user inhales (breathes in)
C. Only when the cabin depressurizes completely
questions.explanation: A demand-type regulator only releases oxygen into the mask when the user actually inhales, conserving oxygen compared with a continuous flow system.

questions.question: If the cabin pressure altitude is the same as the aircraft's actual altitude, what flight mode is this known as?
questions.explanation: When cabin altitude tracks exactly with aircraft altitude (no pressure differential being maintained), the system is operating in unpressurized mode.

questions.question: In the aircraft oxygen system, what color is the discharge indicator typically?
questions.explanation: A green discharge indicator (disk/pin) is the standard color used to show whether the oxygen system's overpressure relief has activated.

questions.question: What is the maximum cabin altitude that can typically be selected using the cabin altitude selector on a pressurized aircraft?
questions.explanation: Pressurization systems are designed so the maximum selectable cabin altitude does not exceed about 10,000 ft, consistent with regulatory cabin altitude limits.

questions.question: Which button scrolls up through the menu options during a BITE test?
questions.explanation: Standard BITE interface controls include dedicated up/down buttons for navigating through test menus and results.

questions.question: What is the typical operating range of cabin differential pressure on a pressurized transport aircraft?
questions.explanation: Transport category aircraft are commonly designed for maximum cabin differential pressures in the range of roughly 3.5 to 9 psi, depending on the specific aircraft type.

questions.question: What type of oxygen is typically used for the flight deck (crew) oxygen system?
questions.explanation: Flight crew oxygen systems commonly use stored high-pressure gaseous oxygen, supplying quick-donning masks with a demand or pressure-demand regulator.

questions.question: What term describes a measure of pressure in a container or line as compared to ambient pressure?
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure is referenced to local ambient (atmospheric) pressure as its zero point, as opposed to absolute pressure, which is referenced to a true vacuum.

questions.question: What factor affects the severity of impairment caused by oxygen deficiency (hypoxia)?
options: A. The duration of the oxygen deficiency
B. The color of the cabin interior
C. The brand of the oxygen mask
questions.explanation: How long the body is deprived of adequate oxygen is a key factor (along with altitude) determining the severity of hypoxia's physiological effects.

questions.question: To which area is gaseous oxygen typically NOT supplied?
options: C. Passenger seating areas (via drop-down masks)
questions.explanation: Standard gaseous oxygen distribution serves the flight deck and passenger seating areas; lavatories are not typically equipped with the main gaseous oxygen distribution supply (though they may have their own separate emergency provision in some designs).

questions.question: When ambient/system temperature increases, what happens to the oxygen level reading in a fixed-volume storage system?
options: A. The pressure gauge reading increases even though the actual oxygen quantity (mass) remains the same
B. The oxygen level (quantity) itself increases
C. The oxygen level (quantity) itself decreases
questions.explanation: Gas pressure is temperature-dependent (per the gas laws); as temperature rises, pressure gauge readings rise even though the actual mass of oxygen stored hasn't changed.

questions.question: What two pressures are compared in the sensing function of the cabin pressure control system?
options: A. Cabin pressure and atmospheric (ambient) pressure
B. Fuel pressure and oil pressure
C. Hydraulic pressure and pneumatic pressure
questions.explanation: The pressurization controller continuously compares cabin pressure against outside atmospheric pressure to determine the appropriate outflow valve position.

questions.question: At cruise altitude, which mode of pressurization control is typically used?
questions.explanation: Once the maximum isobaric cabin altitude limit is reached during climb, the system transitions to constant differential mode, maintaining a fixed pressure differential through cruise.

questions.question: At approximately what aircraft altitude does the pressurization system typically toggle/transition its outflow valve control logic?
questions.explanation: Certain pressurization control logic references specific altitude thresholds (such as around 14,500 ft) for mode transitions or valve scheduling, depending on the aircraft type.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT used as an input to the cabin pressure control system?
questions.explanation: Airspeed is not a direct input the pressurization controller uses; it relies on cabin pressure, landing field altitude, and rate settings instead.

questions.question: What happens once the maximum cabin differential pressure limit is reached?
options: A. The outflow valve closes completely and stays closed
B. The system maintains that maximum differential pressure as the aircraft continues to climb
C. Cabin altitude begins to climb at the same rate as the aircraft
questions.explanation: Once differential pressure reaches its design maximum, the controller holds that value steady, allowing cabin altitude to continue rising slowly in proportion to further aircraft climb.

questions.question: When does the outflow valve remain fully open, with no pressure buildup occurring?
questions.explanation: In unpressurized mode, the outflow valve stays open, allowing cabin pressure to simply track ambient pressure with no differential maintained.

questions.question: What component is used when differential pressure cannot otherwise be maintained and must be actively controlled?
options: C. The dump valve alone, as a steady-state control
questions.explanation: The outflow valve is the primary, continuously modulated component used to actively control and maintain the proper cabin differential pressure.

questions.question: At what altitude does a diluter-demand oxygen regulator typically begin delivering 100% oxygen (no dilution with cabin air)?
questions.explanation: As altitude (and thus available oxygen partial pressure) decreases, the diluter-demand regulator progressively reduces air dilution, delivering 100% oxygen above roughly 35,000 ft.

questions.question: What is the term for pressure testing the fuselage for air leakage while the aircraft is stationary on the ground?
questions.explanation: A static pressure/leak test pressurizes the parked, stationary aircraft to check for leaks, verifying the integrity of seals and structure before return to service.

questions.question: The demand-type oxygen system is specifically designed for use by whom?
questions.explanation: Demand-type oxygen regulators, which conserve oxygen by only delivering it on inhalation, are typically provided for flight crew who may need extended oxygen use.

questions.question: When the external (ambient) pressure decreases to within about 0.25 psi of the selected flight altitude's target pressure, what flight phase is this generally associated with?
options: B. Cruise (reaching the target cruise differential pressure)
questions.explanation: As the aircraft approaches its selected cruise altitude, the differential pressure converges toward the target cruise value, consistent with the transition into cruise flight.

questions.question: What action causes a drop-down passenger oxygen mask to start oxygen flow?
options: A. Pulling the mask (toward the face), which activates the flow lanyard/valve
C. Pressing a separate button on the seatback
questions.explanation: Passenger drop-down masks are designed so that pulling the mask toward the face tugs a lanyard that opens the flow valve, starting oxygen delivery.

questions.question: What determines the maximum allowable cabin differential pressure for an aircraft?
options: C. Structural integrity considerations (fuselage design strength)
questions.explanation: Maximum differential pressure is set by the fuselage's structural design limits, ensuring the pressurized shell isn't overstressed.

questions.question: In hotter weather, how does the pressure gauge reading of an oxygen bottle typically compare with a cooler day, for the same actual oxygen quantity?
questions.explanation: Higher ambient temperature increases the gas pressure reading for a fixed quantity of stored oxygen (per the ideal gas law), even though the actual oxygen mass is unchanged.

questions.question: Setting the target cabin pressure directly affects which component's operation?
questions.explanation: The pressurization controller translates the selected cabin pressure/altitude target into commands that position the outflow valve accordingly.

questions.question: When repairing/servicing an oxygen system, what receives maximum attention?
options: A. The paint finish of fittings
B. Cleanliness of components (to avoid oxygen-fire hazards from oil/grease contamination)
C. The color of the tubing
questions.explanation: Oxygen systems demand strict cleanliness because oil, grease, or other contaminants can spontaneously ignite in the presence of high-pressure oxygen, so cleanliness is a top safety priority during repair.

questions.question: Which component found on/associated with the outflow valve is used to help clear smoke from the cabin or cockpit?
questions.explanation: The dump valve, often integrated near the outflow valve, can be activated to rapidly vent cabin air (and smoke) to help clear a smoke-filled cabin or cockpit.

questions.question: What does the quantity of bleed air directed into the cabin depend on?
options: A. The color of the cabin interior
B. The number of passengers on board
questions.explanation: Fresh air ventilation requirements scale with occupancy, so the bleed/fresh air quantity supplied is set based on the number of passengers to be carried.

questions.question: What limits the flow of oxygen reaching the mask in a continuous flow system?
questions.explanation: A calibrated orifice meters and limits the continuous oxygen flow rate delivered to each passenger mask, matching flow to altitude-appropriate requirements.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the standard operating modes in a pressurization system?
questions.explanation: While the system behaves differently on the ground (outflow/dump valve open via the squat switch), "ground mode" is not usually classified as one of the formal pressurization control modes alongside unpressurized, isobaric, and differential.

questions.question: Which of the following units is an electronic control unit (an ESD-sensitive device) in the pressurization system?
options: A. The outflow valve mechanism itself
C. The dump valve mechanism itself
questions.explanation: The cabin pressure controller is the electronic "brain" of the system and, being electronic, is sensitive to electrostatic discharge (ESD) during handling.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the discharge indication disk on an oxygen bottle?
options: A. To indicate the oxygen purity level
B. To show if overpressure has occurred in the system (the disk ruptures to relieve pressure and signal the event)
C. To indicate the bottle's manufacturing date
questions.explanation: The discharge disk ruptures if the bottle experiences overpressure, both relieving the excess pressure and providing a visual indication that this event occurred.

questions.question: When cabin altitude exceeds roughly 35,000 ft equivalent, what component closes the diluter path in the regulator to supply 100% oxygen?
questions.explanation: An aneroid capsule within the diluter-demand regulator senses the reduced ambient pressure (high cabin altitude) and mechanically shuts off the dilution air path, ensuring 100% oxygen delivery.

questions.question: The cabin is normally pressurized to maintain cabin air pressure equivalent to approximately what altitude?
questions.explanation: Standard cabin pressurization design targets maintaining a cabin altitude of about 8,000 ft or lower during normal cruise, balancing structural limits with occupant comfort/safety.

questions.question: Which component can be operated both automatically and manually?
questions.explanation: The outflow valve is designed to be positioned automatically by the controller in normal operation, but it can also be manually controlled by the crew if needed.

questions.question: What is the lowest cabin altitude that can typically be selected/leveled on a pressurization system?
options: A. About 10,000 ft above sea level
B. About 1,000 ft below sea level
C. About 0 ft (sea level) exactly, with no negative capability
questions.explanation: Pressurization systems commonly allow selecting a cabin altitude slightly below sea level (such as around -1,000 ft) to accommodate airports at low or below-sea-level elevations.

questions.question: What does a cabin pressurization (static/ground) test check?
options: A. The accuracy of the fuel gauges
B. The integrity and sealing of the fuselage
C. The alignment of the landing gear
questions.explanation: This ground test verifies that the fuselage structure and its seals can hold pressure properly, confirming there are no significant leaks before flight.

questions.question: The position of which component can be observed/monitored from the cockpit?
options: A. The dump valve's internal seal wear
C. The reducer valve's internal spring tension
questions.explanation: Cockpit instrumentation (or synoptic displays on modern aircraft) can show outflow valve position, giving the crew visibility into the pressurization system's status.

questions.question: Which statement is true regarding the pressure demand type of oxygen system?
options: A. It supplies oxygen at a lower pressure than diluter demand
B. It supplies oxygen to the mask at a higher pressure than a diluter demand type system
C. It cannot be used by flight crew
questions.explanation: Pressure demand regulators can deliver oxygen under positive pressure into the mask, providing effective oxygenation at very high cabin altitudes, unlike the lower-pressure diluter demand type.

questions.question: A contaminated oxygen system is normally purged using what?
options: C. Oxygen itself (flushing the system with clean oxygen)
questions.explanation: Purging a contaminated oxygen system is done using clean oxygen to flush out contaminants, since introducing other gases (like shop air, which can carry oil/moisture) could worsen contamination risk.

questions.question: What component prevents the aircraft cabin pressure from becoming greater (in the reverse sense) than ambient, i.e., prevents cabin pressure from dropping below outside pressure?
options: A. The negative pressure relief valve
B. The positive pressure relief valve
questions.explanation: The negative relief valve opens if outside (ambient) pressure exceeds cabin pressure, preventing a damaging reverse (negative) pressure differential on the fuselage.

questions.question: What is the expected purity level of aviation (breathing) oxygen?
questions.explanation: Aviation breathing oxygen specifications require very high purity, typically around 99.5% or greater, to ensure safe and effective physiological performance.

questions.question: If cabin pressure varies at an equal rate with ambient pressure (maintaining a fixed differential), the aircraft is operating in what mode?
questions.explanation: When cabin pressure changes in lockstep with ambient pressure, maintaining a fixed pressure difference, the system is in constant (steady) differential pressure mode.

questions.question: During ground operation of the pressurization system, what controls the outflow/dump valve to be held open?
questions.explanation: The WOW switch senses that the aircraft is on the ground and holds the relevant valve(s) open to keep the cabin unpressurized during ground operations.

questions.question: In an all-pneumatic cabin pressure regulator and outflow valve system, which is a pressure sense line connection?
questions.explanation: In older, fully pneumatic pressurization control designs, the dump valve's sensing connection provides the pressure reference signal used by the regulating logic.

questions.question: Which valve ensures the structural integrity of the aircraft is protected if pressurization control is lost (preventing overpressure)?
options: A. The negative pressure relief valve
B. The positive pressure relief valve
questions.explanation: A positive pressure relief valve opens automatically if cabin pressure rises too high (exceeding the maximum differential), protecting the fuselage structure from overpressure damage.

questions.question: In a demand regulator, which component meters/delivers 100% oxygen above approximately 34,000 feet?
options: B. The diluter-demand regulator (via its altitude-sensing aneroid mechanism)
questions.explanation: The diluter-demand regulator's internal aneroid mechanism progressively shuts off cabin air dilution as altitude increases, delivering 100% oxygen above roughly 34,000 ft.

questions.question: Why is a continuous flow oxygen system considered a wasteful design?
options: A. Because it uses too little oxygen to be effective
B. Because it requires electrical power to operate
C. Because oxygen is wasted (continues flowing) even if the user is not actively consuming/inhaling it
questions.explanation: Unlike demand systems that release oxygen only on inhalation, continuous flow systems release a steady stream regardless of the user's breathing cycle, wasting oxygen during exhalation.
